value.body: A B.Com that adds computing papers to the usual commerce core — run as a named B.Com (Computer Applications) programme at many universities. Alongside financial accounting, tax, business law and economics, you study computerised accounting, office and spreadsheet tools, database basics and SQL, a programming language, and web or e-commerce fundamentals. The exact computing papers vary a lot by university.

items.label: B.Com students (all specialisations)
items.note: All modes; the higher figure includes B.Com (Hons)

items.label: Software usually taught
items.value: Accounting software, spreadsheets, a database and a programming language
items.note: The language (for example C, Java or Python) depends on the university

value.title: How you get in
value.body: Class 12 (commerce preferred, not always required). Central and many other universities admit through CUET-UG; others admit on Class 12 marks or their own process. Some universities set subject conditions for this programme, such as Mathematics or Computer Science in Class 12; check the prospectus. Where it is a named programme, you choose it at admission.

value.title: At a glance
items: It remains a commerce degree; software-developer roles usually need further study, and an MCA is the common bridge (most MCA programmes ask for Mathematics at Class 12 or graduation).
Entry-level work is often accounts executive on accounting software or ERP, MIS and reporting, back-office operations, or IT support.
Spreadsheet and SQL skills are frequently tested in hiring for reporting and analyst roles.
Common next steps: an MCA, M.Com or MBA, or a CA/CMA course alongside the degree.
